analysis.one_liner: Writes the Roe v. Wade abortion standard and contraception rights into federal law.
analysis.headline: Introduced days after a bipartisan group of four senators, the bill to restore the Roe v. Wade standard never got a hearing or a vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in Dobbs (2022), this bill would have written the old Roe and Casey rules into federal statute: states could not ban abortion before fetal viability, could not ban contraception, and could not ban an abortion needed to protect a woman's life or health even after viability. It also let the Justice Department or any person hurt by a violating state law go to court to stop that law, with attorney's fees available to the winner. It was introduced by a bipartisan group of four senators but never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Women of reproductive age, especially those in states that moved to ban or severely restrict abortion after Dobbs, would have regained a guaranteed federal right to abortion before fetal viability and to contraception. Abortion and contraception providers would have gained a stable federal legal standard protecting them from state prosecution and clinic shutdowns.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars states from prohibiting abortion before fetal viability and from imposing an 'undue burden' — a substantial obstacle — on a woman's choice to end a pregnancy, restoring the standard the Supreme Court applied under Roe and Casey [S2][S3].
It bars states from prohibiting individuals from obtaining or using contraceptives, codifying the contraception holdings of Griswold, Eisenstadt, and Carey [S2][S3].
Even after fetal viability, a state may not prohibit an abortion that the attending doctor judges medically necessary to protect the woman's life or health [S2][S3].

The Justice Department or any person adversely affected by a violating state law can seek a court order blocking that law, and the prevailing party can recover attorney's fees — a practical enforcement tool for individuals who could not otherwise afford to sue [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: States that restrict abortion would lose that authority before fetal viability, and state laws regulating abortion clinics could be struck down in court if they created a substantial obstacle. Taxpayer-funded federal litigation by the Justice Department could also increase.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state abortion laws nationwide before fetal viability, removing the ability of state governments — and the voters who elect them — to set their own rules, a federalism cost its opponents considered fundamental [S2][S3].

By codifying the Whole Woman's Health v. Hellerstedt holding, the bill lets courts strike down state clinic health-and-safety regulations that create a substantial obstacle, which critics argued would block states from regulating abortion facilities at all [S2][S3].

The bill leaves the post-viability standard to the attending practitioner's judgment of 'life or health,' a standard opponents argued is broad enough to make post-viability limits hard to enforce [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who support legal abortion, the benefits are large and direct: a guaranteed federal floor that no state can cut below, enforceable in court. The costs are real but different in kind: it takes regulatory authority away from states, and its health-and-safety and post-viability limits leave room for argument about how far state rules can go. The bill does not create new funding, does not mandate anything for individuals, and explicitly preserves conscience protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 1, 2022, weeks after the Dobbs decision returned abortion regulation to the states, by Sen. Tim Kaine joined by Sens. Murkowski, Collins, and Sinema — a bipartisan, four-sponsor introduction [S1][S3].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which is where its action history ends [S1][S5].
No committee markup, hearing, floor vote, or further chamber action appears anywhere in the bill's record for the remainder of the Congress [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments that restrict abortion kept full authority, since no federal standard replaced state law. Elected officials who opposed a nationwide statutory abortion right avoided having to cast a recorded vote on one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States restricting abortion; officials who avoided a vote

for.name: Sen. Tim Kaine
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to codify the essential holdings of Roe, Casey, Griswold, and related cases

for.name: Sens. Lisa Murkowski, Susan Collins, and Kyrsten Sinema
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, making the bill a bipartisan four-sponsor introduction

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up — no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in its record for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Senate Democratic leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and caucus leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the Senate floor in the remaining five months of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced across party lines — one Democrat, two Republicans, and one independent — but it never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where the parties actually stood.

industries.note: A federal viability standard and court enforcement would shield clinics from state bans and post-Dobbs closures, and let providers and patients sue to block restrictive state laws. Their business survives only where patients can legally reach them.
The bill guarantees a federal right to obtain and use contraception, protecting the market for contraceptive products and services against state-level bans.
